title: 'Gateless Barrier, Case 35: Wu-tsu: "Which Is the True Ch''ien?"'
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: The Soto Zen teacher uses a parable from Chinese folklore to encourage listeners to confront their difficult choices and consider the limitations of conventional wisdom. The story illustrates how our inner conflict can lead to division within us, but also suggests that by embracing both sides of ourselves, we can heal and return to wholeness. This teaching invites listeners to explore their own inner divisions and consider a more nuanced approach to decision-making, one that acknowledges the complexity of human experience rather than relying solely on external guidance or rigid rules.

sentences.text: *An unsurpassed, penetrating, imperfect dharma is rarely met with even in a hundred thousand million kalpas.
Having it to see and listen to, to remember and accept, I vow to taste the truth of the Tathagata's word.*
Okay.
Good evening again, everybody.
Thank you so much for inviting your evening to sangha.
It must be interesting to try to learn our form through the little tiny screens, so very excellent effort, those of you who are learning this through this medium.
I want to say a few things tonight about Mumen Khan case 35, which is based on a pretty interesting Chinese folktale.
The whole of case 35 in the Mumen Khan is just a teacher asking a monk a question.
Here's the case.
*Wuzu said to his monks, "The woman Qian and her spirit separated.
Which was the real Qian?"*
Wuzu was the teacher.
Wutsu, I guess, said to his monks, "The woman Qian and her spirit separated.
Which is the real Qian?"
This character Qian is a reference to a woman in Chinese mythology.
Here's the story.
It's a folktale.
*There lived in the Han Yang a man called Qian, whose child daughter Qian was a peerless beauty.*
They're always peerless beauties.
*He also had a nephew named Chou, who was a very handsome boy.
The two children played together and were very fond of each other.
Once Qian, the dad of Qian, justly said to his nephew, "Someday I will marry you to my little daughter."
And both children remembered these words and they believed themselves would be betrothed.*
So we have three characters so far.
Qian is the dad.
Qian is the daughter and Chou is the nephew.
*When Qian grew up, once Qian grew up, a man of rank asked for her in marriage.
And her father decided to comply with the demand.
Qian was greatly troubled by this decision.
As for Chou, he was so much angered and aggrieved that he resolved to leave home and go to another province.
So the next day he got the boat ready for his journey.
And after sunset, without bidding farewell to anyone, he proceeded up the river.
But in the middle of the night, he was startled by a voice calling to him.
"Wait!
It is I!"
He saw a girl running along the bank towards the boat.
He guessed it.
It was Qian.
Chou was completely unspeakably delighted.
She sprang into the boat and the lovers found their way safely to the province of Chou.
And in the province of Chou they lived happily for six years.
And they had two children.
But Qian could not forget her parents and often longed to see them again.
At last he said to her husband,*
*"Because in former times I could not bear to break the promise made to you, I ran away with you and forsook my parents.
Although knowing that I owed them all possible duty and affection, would it not be well to try to obtain their forgiveness?"
"Do not grieve about that," said Chou.
"We shall go to see them."
So he ordered the boat to be prepared.
And a few days later he returned with his wife to Hanyang, where they came from.*
*According to custom in such cases, the husband first went to the house of Qian, leaving Qian alone in the boat.
Qian welcomed his nephew with every sign of joy and said, "How much I have been longing to see you.
I was often afraid that something bad had happened to you."
Chou answered respectfully, "I am distressed by the undeserved kindness of your words."*
This is the nephew who ran off with this guy's daughter.
*"Because it is to beg your forgiveness that I have come."
But Qian didn't seem to understand.
He said, "To what manner do you refer?"
"I feared," said Chou, "that you would be angry with me for having run away with Qian.
I took her with me to the province of Chou."
"What Qian was that?" asked Qian.
"Your daughter, Qian," answered Chou, beginning to suspect his father-in-law of some malevolent design.
"What are you talking about?" cried Qian, the daughter, with every appearance of astonishment.
"My daughter Qian has been sick in bed all these years, ever since the time when you went away."*
She's been sick in bed.
*"Your daughter, Qian," returned Chou, becoming angry, "has not been sick.
She's been my wife for six years, and we have two children, and we've now returned to this place only to seek your pardon.
Therefore, please do not mock us."
For a moment, the two looked at each other in silence.
Then Qian the dad arose and motioned his nephew to follow, and led the way to an inner room where a sick girl was lying.
And Chou, to his utter amazement, saw the face of Qian, beautiful but strangely thin and pale.
"She cannot speak," explained the old man, "but she can understand."*
*And then he said to her laughingly, "Chou here tells me that you ran away with him.
You have two children.
Isn't that ridiculous?"
The sick girl looked at Chou and smiled, but remained silent.
"Now come with me to the river," said the bewildered visitor to his father-in-law.
"For I can assure you, in spite of what I have seen in this house, that your daughter, Qian, is at this moment in my boat."
So they went to the river, and there indeed was the young wife, waiting.
Seeing her father, she bowed down before him and sought his pardon.
Qian said to her, "If you really are my daughter, I have nothing but love for you.
Yet though you seem to be my daughter, there is something which I cannot understand.
Come with us to the house."
So the three proceeded towards the house.
As they neared it, they saw the sick girl, who had not before left her bed for all those years,*
*that she had gotten up and was coming to meet them, smiling as if much delighted.
And the two Qian's approached each other.
And then, nobody could ever tell how, they suddenly melted into each other and became one body, one person.
One Qian.
Even more beautiful than before, and showing no sign of sickness or sorrow.
Then Qian, the dad, said to Chou,*
*"Ever since the day of your going, my daughter was dumb, unable to speak.
And most of the time, like a person who has taken too much wine.
Now I know that her spirit was absent."
Qian said, herself said, "Really I never knew, really I never knew that I was at home.
I saw Chou going away in silent anger, and the same night I dreamed that I ran after his boat.
But now I cannot tell which was really I, I that went away in the boat, or the I that stayed at home."*
So that's the far out story of the two Qian's, or the split Qian.
Back to our case, the Zen teacher is referring to this, talking to a student, and he asks, which was the real one?
Which is the real one?
Here we have someone faced with an impossible choice, right?
A choice between love and passion on the one hand, and a vision of the future that she and her betrothed had long, long held, right?
To where it was completely real.
And the choice to do the correct thing, right?
To do the conventional thing, to be obedient, which is especially a big deal in that society, as I understand it.
The stress of that choice is so powerful that it split her in two, like ripped her in twos.
And one half of her spirit went off with her childhood sweetheart, Chou.
Ran off, started a new life together, had a family.
And the other half stayed with the father, and the stress of the spirit running off in this story left the remaining part of her frail and ill, without words, unable to speak.
Presumably the arranged marriage to the man of rank never happened when she got sick; it doesn't say.
So it really makes you think about difficult choices.
Every one of us has faced difficult choices.
Sometimes with this particular valence, the wild pull between passion and convention, but it's all kinds of things that pull us apart, right?
Where we want one thing and we know we should do the other, or we want the other, or we want both.
And I think, though, I don't know if I totally agree with one symbol in the story.
It doesn't seem like the conventional and correct necessarily makes us sick, though it could.
But is it more usual that the conventional and the correct is fine, but it's only just fine, it's limited?
It's flat in some way, it doesn't really support us in manifesting fully our rich selves.
As the process of our being gets lost, we're going through the motions, doing what we're supposed to.
All of us have had periods like that in our lives, I'm sure.
But on the other hand, the wild and the passionate, the visionary, the going for it side of us, it may be exciting and energizing, but it's unbalanced.
Also not quite right.
Keon in the story regretted her actions and sought forgiveness from her parents for six years, wondered if she would ever see them again.
I mean, it sounds like she had a pretty nice six years with her wonderful husband and the two lovely kids, but it wasn't quite right.
And so she had to return, right, so it's another spiritual story of the way we always have to return home in the end.
I think what's most fascinating to me this time in this story, and I thought of this before, was the way the two Keons come together at the end.
That the spirit Keon, driven by regret and desire for forgiveness, has to return home, that makes sense.
But her returning home isn't just for her benefit, it also awakens her ill other, empowers the part of her that stayed behind.
And I wonder, too, about this story with the illness.
Would the spirit Keon eventually have gotten sick anyway, through this unresolved situation that she'd created for herself?
The imbalance of running away like that.
And maybe we've all, to some extent, been spiritually, emotionally, physically sick as a result of clinging to one path, clinging to one half of something.
But then the super interesting thing is the sick, sort of husk of her, when the spirit of her returns, gets up.
After six years of lying there, not speaking.
And so that's really fascinating, that they re-empowered each other and that there was not a note, and they didn't turn away from each other either.
They turned towards each other.
So these two cleaved, separated halves turned towards each other.
I was thinking about that, just sort of psychologically.
Can we look inside and see a part of ourself that's ashamed, regrets our choice, doesn't really want to be seen?
And it's so easy to ignore that part of ourselves, right?
To ignore the part of us that has done or is doing something that we're embarrassed by, ashamed of.
Easy to bury that or belittle it.
Or there's so many strategies we have to try to avoid the many ways that we're suffering from our internal divisions, right?
And of course the strategies for avoiding that usually just lead to more suffering.
So that's one half.
I think that's interesting, this turning towards the embarrassment and shame of having abandoned her family.
But then the other part I think is really interesting is this sad, ill, remaining part of her.
That it allows itself, she allows herself to be inspired and wake back up, and that's hard for us too, right?
When you're depressed or sad, don't you think there's a part of you that just wants to turn away from happiness and joy and delight?
So that part of her is awakened as well.
And as the story says:
*As they neared the house, they saw the sick girl who had not before left her bed for years was coming to meet them, smiling as if much delighted.
And the two Keons approached each other.
And then, nobody could ever tell how, they suddenly melted into each other and became one body, one person, one Keon, even more beautiful than before and showing no signs of sickness or sorrow.*
So the stress of a big choice, whether it's around this particular issue of love and societal norms or some other huge issue, the stress is huge, right?
It pulls us apart.
Neither choice is quite right, so how do we navigate that?
And once we've split and we're imbalanced, how do we eventually find our way back to the part of ourselves that we've abandoned and left behind?
How do we return to wholeness?
And in the koan, the teacher asks the student, which of you is real, right?
Which of you is true?
Which of you is Tim or Terrell or Das or Judith, or which of you is the real you?
Is it one?
Is it the other?
Is it both?
Is it neither?
Is it something bigger than that question?
And the poem that Master Muman, who put the book together, wrote for this is kind of interesting, I think.
Here's the poem for the koan from Master Muman.
*The moon and the clouds are the same.
The mountains and valleys are different.
All are blessed.
All are blessed.
Is this one?
Is this two?*
*The moon and the clouds are the same.
Mountains and valleys are different.
All are blessed.
All are blessed.
Is this one?
Is this two?*
*The moon and the clouds are the same.*
Up in the sky, on a cloudy moonlit night, where does the moon end?
Where do the clouds start?
Can clouds and moons divide?
Can you divide?
Or aren't all these parts of you just aspects of the same?
The same you-ness?
*The mountains and valleys are different.*
A mountain is a mountain.
A valley is a valley.
This part of you is this part, and that part is that part.
There's different voices in there, as I'm sure you've noticed.
And of course, that's how it is.
How could it be otherwise?
As Master Shitou says in our other poem, if you're confused, mountains and rivers block your way, right?
So there's separation.
And along with that separation, there's confusion.
There's separation.
*All are blessed.
All are blessed.*
So that's interesting.
Not the usual kind of grouchy talk.
Grouchy Zen talk is usually in these poems from Master Wu Men.
There's a sweetness here, a blessing, a coming together, a wholeness, a beauty.
And it's said that when Kian came back together, she was more beautiful even than before.
Someone actually told me the other day that I look younger.
So maybe parts of me have come back together or something.
I hope so.
That'd be nice.
Some restless energy coming back, coming back home.
Healing the sick parts of me.
Wouldn't that be good for all of us?
We all have many divided Kians in us.
Little by little, they'll all come back, we hope.
And we'll all be more beautiful than before.
Which is kind of like one of the things that's fun at the end of a long retreat.
You look around and everybody does look younger and more beautiful, softer.
It's the same faces, but they look different somehow.
So maybe over the course of our intents of Zazen, we do something like what this story describes.
*Is this one?
Is this two?*
It's just one life, really.
And yet there are all these different things and ideas and actions internally and externally, right?
And does what divides us help us?
Because in the end we can return home to find our wholeness.
Or were we one all along?
*Is this one?
Is this two?*
So that's all I wanted to say about case 35.
Which is the true Qian, or Qian.
I don't know if some Chinese person helped me with the name pronunciation.
I think I was kind of wrong, but that's all right.
You got the point.
